name: Executive order of May 21, 1883 keeping the north half of Camp Harney (320 acres) as the last of the Malheur Reservation
nations: Wadatika and other Snake or Paiute bands of the Malheur country (Northern Paiute), today the Burns Paiute Tribe
promises: Not a treaty: a presidential order. It retained for a future reserve the north half of the Camp Harney military reservation, 320 acres (Royce p. 912, area 647).

Royce says the Camp Harney military reservation, 640 acres, had been made part of the Indian reservation on July 23, 1880, and that its south half went with the order of September 13, 1882 (Royce pp. 910 and 913).

breaches.what: The Commission found the bands were deprived of their title to the Malheur Reservation land in January 1879, when the United States forcibly removed them to the Yakima Reservation and restored the land to the public domain without their consent or payment. Finding 37 records that by an executive order of March 2, 1889 the 320-acre tract was also restored to the public domain, that none of the land within the reservation was sold for the bands' benefit, and that they were never compensated.

landTaken: The 320-acre north half of Camp Harney, restored to the public domain by executive order of March 2, 1889 (Commission finding 37).
compensation: The Commission valued the land at $579,722.00 as of January 1879, less offsets (Second Interlocutory Order, April 15, 1959). Interior described the judgment as $567,000 and said fees and expenses reduced it to $468,395.50, which with interest stood at $519,827.49 on June 5, 1963 (press release, 1963).
today: The Burns Paiute Tribe lives near Burns, Oregon, on the edge of the former reservation (Commission finding 38). This is the same January 1879 taking already recorded under cession-1872-09-12-paiute-shoshone-snake and the other Malheur entries; it is counted once. The 1889 order is also in the queue as cession-1889-03-02-malheur-indian-reservation-shoshone-snak (area 647).

nationVoice.summary: The Tribe says its ancestors refused to cede any of their lands, that the Malheur executive order reservation of 1.8 million acres was short-lived, and that after the Bannock War the survivors were marched over 300 miles in deep snow to Fort Simcoe and Fort Vancouver.

openQuestions: Same land and event as cession-1872-09-12-paiute-shoshone-snake (the January 1879 taking, Docket 17); counted once. This order itself kept the 320 acres; they were lost by the order of March 2, 1889, which the queue also carries (cession-1889-03-02-malheur-indian-reservation-shoshone-snak, same area 647) and which should point to the same primary.

Whether the Camp Harney tract lay inside the January 28, 1876 boundaries the Commission valued (finding 3) was not checked; the 1872 order excepted the Camp Harney military reserve, and Royce says it joined the Indian reservation only in 1880. Finding 37 covers the 320 acres by name.

plain.promised: Not a treaty. This 1883 order kept 320 acres at old Camp Harney as all that was left of the Malheur Reservation for the Paiute bands.
plain.happened: The Indian Claims Commission found those 320 acres were also restored to the public domain in 1889 and the bands were never paid for any reservation land. Interior admitted in 1963 no compensation was paid.
plain.today: The Commission valued the land at $579,722.00; Interior described a $567,000 judgment. This is the same taking shown on the other Malheur entries.
